source_text: Ἀλλ᾿ οὐδὲ θυσίαις πολλαῖς καὶ πλοκαῖς ἀνθῶν τιμῶμεν, οὓς ἄνθρωποι μορφώσαντες καὶ ἐν ναοῖς ἱδρύσαντες θεοὺς προσωνόμασαν, ἐπεὶ ἄψυχα καὶ νεκρὰ ταῦτα γινώσκομεν καὶ θεοῦ μορφὴν μὴ ἔχοντα (οὐ γὰρ τοιαύτην ἡγούμεθα τὸν θεὸν ἔχειν τὴν μορφήν, ἣν φασί τινες εἰς τιμὴν μεμιμῆσθαι), ἀλλ᾿ ἐκείνων τῶν φανέντων κακῶν δαιμόνων καὶ ὀνόματα καὶ σχήματα ἔχειν. Τί γὰρ δεῖ εἰδόσιν ὑμῖν λέγειν, ἃ τὴν ὕλην οἱ τεχνῖται διατιθέασι ξέοντες καὶ τέμνοντες καὶ χωνεύοντες καὶ τύπτοντες; Καὶ ἐξ ἀτίμων πολλάκις σκευῶν διὰ τέχνης τὸ σχῆμα μόνον ἀλλάξαντες καὶ μορφοποιήσαντες θεοὺς ἐπονομάζουσιν. Ὅπερ οὐ μόνον ἄλογον ἡγούμεθα, ἀλλὰ καὶ ἐφ᾿ ὕβρει τοῦ θεοῦ γίνεσθαι, ὃς ἄῤῥητον δόξαν καὶ μορφὴν ἔχων ἐπὶ φθαρτοῖς καὶ δεομένοις θεραπείας πράγμασιν ἐπονομάζεται. Καὶ ὅτι οἱ τούτων τεχνῖται ἀσελγεῖς εἰσι καὶ πᾶσαν κακίαν, ἵνα μὴ καταριθμῶμεν, ἔχουσιν, ἀκριβῶς ἐπίστασθε· καὶ τὰς ἑαυτῶν παιδίσκας συνεργαζομένας φθείρουσιν. Ὤ τῆς ἐμβροντησίας, ἀνθρώπους ἀκολάστους θεοὺς εἰς τὸ προσκυνεῖσθαι πλάσσειν λέγεσθαι καὶ μεταποιεῖν, καὶ τῶν ἱερῶν, ἔνθα ἀνατίθενται, φύλακας τοιούτους καθιστάναι, μὴ συνορῶντας ἀθέμιτον καὶ τὸ νοεῖν ἢ λέγειν ἀνθρώπους θεῶν εἶναι φύλακας.
pass_a_gloss: But neither with many sacrifices and braids of flowers do we honor those whom men having shaped and having established in temples have named gods, since we know these things to be inanimate and dead and not having the form of God (for we do not consider God to have such a form as some say has been imitated in honor), but rather to have the names and shapes of those apparent evil demons. For what need is there for me to tell you things which you know, which the craftsmen assign to the material, shaping and cutting and hollowing and beating? And from worthless things often, having changed only the shape through craft and having shaped, they name them gods. Which we consider not only irrational, but also to happen because of the insult of God, who having unspeakable glory and form is named over perishable and needy things. And that the craftsmen of these things are licentious and have all wickedness, so that I may not enumerate, you know accurately; and they corrupt their own servant girls who work together with them. Oh the shamelessness, that lawless men are said to fashion and transform into gods to be worshiped, and to establish such guards of the sacred things, where they are placed, not seeing that it is unlawful and to think or say that men are guards of gods.

choices.english: because of the insult of God

pass_b_english: We do not honor the images that human beings have carved and set up in temples with crowds of sacrifices and garlands of flowers. We know that such objects are lifeless and dead, and that they lack the form of God. We do not believe that God possesses the kind of form that some claim these statues imitate in his honor; on the contrary, these images bear the names and shapes of the evil demons that have appeared. Why should I describe for you what you already know: the way craftsmen work the material, melting, cutting, casting, and hammering it? They often take worthless substances and, by changing nothing but the outward shape through their art, call the results gods. We regard this not only as irrational but as an insult to God, who possesses unspeakable glory and form, yet is named over perishable things that need constant care. You know perfectly well that the artisans who make these idols are licentious and steeped in every kind of wickedness, so much so that I need not list it all; they even corrupt the servant girls who work beside them. Oh, the shamelessness of it: lawless men are said to fashion and transform objects into gods to be worshiped, and then appoint such men as guardians of the sacred places where the idols stand, never perceiving that it is unlawful even to think or say that human beings could be guardians of gods.

review.notes: The translation accurately captures the nuances of the Greek text. Pass A provides a literal rendering of the clauses, and Pass B provides a fluent English version that maintains the semantic integrity of the original, including the technical descriptions of the craftsmen's work (melting, cutting, casting, hammering) and the theological distinctions regarding God's glory versus the perishable nature of idols.

The translation accurately reflects the Greek text, with no omissions, additions, or distortions. The cited scripture is not present in this passage, but the translation does not claim to include it. The title 'Idolatry' appropriately captures the content of the passage. The translation preserves the meaning, agency, negation, modality, and doctrine of the original Greek text. The source is correctly identified as Justin's First Apology 9. The translation is faithful to the original text, with no errors in the representation of the Greek content.
